question: Does a monthly Labour Force Survey result describe what respondents did throughout the whole month?
generated_answer: The Labour Force Survey asks respondents about their activities during the week preceding the Sunday of the interview. You should not assume that the entire month was spent in the same activity. For example, a respondent may have been unemployed for the entire month of February, but that does not necessarily imply they were unemployed for the first 3 weeks and employed for the last week, or employed for the first 3 weeks and unemployed for the last week. If a person who is not working did not actively look for work during the reference week, they are counted as not in the labour force, even if they want a job. A person is considered employed if they had a paid job during the week of the LFS reference week. This includes not only wage and salary positions but also self-employment, casual work and unpaid family work. How is unemployment measured? Unemployment data from the LFS are based on a shorter reference period, the week of the LFS interview. This is why the numbers may seem different from Statistics Canada’s Labour Force Survey (LFS). The LFS counts a person as unemployed if they did not have a job but actively looked for work in the previous four weeks, and were available to work. In contrast, the LFS counts a person as unemployed if they did not have a job but actively looked for work only in the previous week. What is the difference between the unemployment rate and the unemployment rate excluding discouraged workers? The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed divided by the total number of people in the labour force (employed and unemployed). In order to be considered unemployed, a person must have been actively seeking employment in the previous four weeks. People who have become discouraged about their chances of finding work and have given up looking are not counted as unemployed, even though they would be if they were considered to be in the labour force. How is the unemployment rate different from the underutilization rate? The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed divided by the total number of people in the labour force (employed and unemployed). How is employment measured? Employment data from the LFS are based on a shorter reference period, the week of the LFS interview. This is why the numbers may seem different from Statistics Canada’s Labour Force Survey (LFS). The LFS counts a person as employed if they had a paid job or if they did any unpaid family work during the week of the LFS reference week. In contrast, the LFS counts a person as employed if they had a paid job or if they did any unpaid family work during the previous four weeks. The employment rate is the number of employed divided by the total number of people who could be in the labour force (employed, unemployed and not in the labour force).
